Building a Unique Tradition
A Bilingual Church of England School in the Heart of Harrow
Our School
Aims & Achievements
We are proud to be different. We were founded by parents with a vision of providing an outstanding and enriching academic education, rooted in Christian values and ethos, that offered the opportunity for a bilingual education beyond the private sector. We are proud to say that we have achieved our founding aspirations and relentlessly pursue our aims. Our academic attainment scores are consistently above the national averages; many of our children achieve Diplomas of French Language Studies DELF PRIM, organised by the French Ministry of Education and recognised worldwide.
Our Vision & Values
Aspiration, Courage, Resilience, Love, Respect, Hope, Joy, Peace, Justice. An aspirational, multilingual, multicultural education community that empowers everyone: to grow and flourish, to gain in knowledge, wisdom and skills and to translate the love of God for all people into words and actions. Our core values are aligned with our founding ethos: to provide a rigorous and outstanding academic curriculum in a Church of England context and offering unique bilingual provision in a state setting. We are highly ambitious for each and every one of our pupils and are dedicated to the holistic flourishing of each child.
A Message from Our Headteacher
Welcome to Saint Jérôme Church of England Bilingual School. I am Kate Schutte, and I am delighted to be leading our wonderful school community.
St Jérôme has a clear Christian vision at its heart. Our faith shapes the values we live by and the way we care for one another, while warmly welcoming children and families of all faiths and none. Alongside this, our pupils learn and grow bilingually in English and French, within a community where they are encouraged to be ambitious, resilient and kind, and to take pride in both their achievements and their character.
I warmly invite you to explore our website to find out more about our curriculum, our community, and what makes St Jérôme such a special place to learn. If you are considering a place for your child, I would be delighted to welcome you for a visit.
Kate Schutte, Headteacher

pageCache.pageTitle: Our Ethos, Our Values | Saint Jérôme Church of England Bilingual School
pageCache.text:
Our Christian Values
Our Christian Values
We seek to be an aspirational, multilingual, multicultural education community that empowers everyone: to grow and flourish, to gain in knowledge, wisdom and skills and to translate the love of God for all people into words and actions.
As a designated Church of England School we have a Christian vision and ethos. We welcome children of all faiths and none.
The Christian faith provides many guiding principles and core ethos and values that can shape a holistic approach to education.
At St. Jérôme Church of England Bilingual School, a Christian ethos and a multi-cultural, multi-lingual approach go hand in hand. We promote integration amongst all people of all different cultures and backgrounds, both within the school and in the wider community. Learning Francophone cultures and customs give children a second way to see the world and help develop them as engaged global citizens.
Within the vision of the school, the beliefs and practices of other faiths are respected. Religious Education reflects the diversity of the local community and promotes reflection and spiritual, moral and cultural development.
To find out more about Religious Education in our school click here.
Notre Ethos
Etant désignée comme école anglicane nous préserverons les valeurs chrétiennes mais nous accueillerons les enfants de toutes confessions ainsi que les non-croyants.
La religion chrétienne fournit de nombreux principes directeurs et valeurs essentielles qui peuvent former une vision holistique de l’éducation.
A l’école anglicane bilingue de St Jérôme, un ethos chrétien et une approche multiculturelle et multi-langue, vont de pair. Nous allons promouvoir l’intégration, parmi toutes les personnes de cultures et d’origines différentes, dans notre école mais aussi dans la communauté. Le fait d’apprendre les cultures et coutumes francophones permettra aux enfants d’acquérir une deuxième vision du monde et les aidera à devenir des citoyens du monde engagés.
Dans le cadre de notre philosophie nous respecterons les croyances et les pratiques d’autres religions. L’éducation religieuse reflétera la diversité de la communauté locale et s’attachera à promouvoir la réflexion et le développement spirituel, moral et culturel.
Our Christian Values
Every September we reflect on the values that we feel all members of the school community should uphold.
Our worship theme for the Michaelmas Term is also based around these values.
At Saint Jérôme, our values take the place of school rules.
Nos valeurs chrétiennes
Chaque septembre, nous réfléchissons aux valeurs que nous avons choisies, respectées par toute notre communauté scolaire.
Notre liturgie du premier trimestre est aussi basée sur nos valeurs.
À St Jérôme, nos valeurs sont aussi nos règles de conduite.
Through our values we will foster a life-long love of learning and independent thought, rather than simply preparing our prospective pupils to sit examinations. This culture will help our children to develop into mature and responsible boys and girls.
St John the Baptist, Greenhill
St Jérôme is proud to have close links with our parish church. To find out more about our relationship with the parish, please see our Parish Church page.

Spiritual Development & Godly Play
Spiritual Development & Godly Play
What is Godly Play?
A creative and imaginative approach to Christian nurture, Godly Play:
It invites listeners into stories and encourages them to connect the stories with personal experience, Godly Play:
Developed originally as a resource for children, Godly Play is now being used with a wide range of age groups in a diversity of settings.
Godly Play is one of several variations of the Montessori tradition of religious education and was developed in the United States by Dr Jerome Berryman. Many of our staff are trained Godly Play practitioners following their training course held at our partner school, Holy Trinity CE Primary School. Northwood.
Values process, openness and discovery
Encourages people to make meaning for themselves
Uses wondering questions and open-ended response time
So what’s a Godly Play Room?
In addition to the usual rooms you would find in any primary school we have a Godly Play Room.
Our Godly Play room is housed on our top floor near our hall. Our room has a deep-pile carpet to make it more comfortable for children to sit on.
Around the room are a number of resources that the Godly Play storyteller uses to tell a story.
Part of the room is not carpeted and this allows children to use creative materials to ‘wonder’ about the story.
We are delighted to show Godly Play practitioners our room and even see a session in action.

pageCache.pageTitle: French | Saint Jérôme Church of England Bilingual School
pageCache.text:
French
Subjects
French
Curriculum Vision Statement
At St Jérôme, our French curriculum reflects our vision of being an aspirational, multilingual and multicultural learning community in which every child is empowered to grow, flourish and communicate with confidence. Through French, pupils develop the knowledge, wisdom and skills needed to engage with the wider world and to translate the love that God has for all people into both words and actions.
French is not simply a subject at St Jérôme; it is part of pupils’ daily experience. From EYFS onwards, children encounter French through songs, stories, classroom routines, acts of worship, special celebrations and meaningful interactions with our francophone community. These experiences foster a love of languages and a deep appreciation of francophone cultures and traditions.
Our curriculum develops pupils’ knowledge of French phonics, vocabulary, grammar and culture alongside the key language skills of listening, speaking, reading and writing. We aim to nurture confident communicators who can understand, respond and express themselves with increasing accuracy and independence.
By the end of Key Stage 2, pupils are equipped to use French in a range of authentic contexts, demonstrate intercultural understanding and continue their language-learning journey with confidence. Many pupils also achieve internationally recognised DELF qualifications, providing formal recognition of their bilingual achievements.
How is French taught at St Jérôme?
French is taught through a combination of structured language lessons, language immersion and bilingual learning experiences across the curriculum. In Key Stage 2, our curriculum is built around the Rachel Hawkes Scheme of Work, which reflects current research into effective language learning and focuses on the key strands of phonics, vocabulary and grammar. The scheme provides a strong foundation which we adapt and enrich through bespoke resources and activities designed to meet the needs of our bilingual learners.
Adaptive teaching is central to our approach. Pupils are taught in streamed groups according to their current level of French proficiency rather than their age or year group. This enables teachers to provide appropriate support and challenge, ensuring that all pupils make strong progress from their individual starting points. Our wealth of francophone staff allows us to tailor learning experiences and respond effectively to pupils’ varying language needs.
Oracy lies at the heart of our French curriculum. Pupils are encouraged to speak French every day through classroom routines, partner discussions, role play, presentations, songs and structured speaking activities. Regular opportunities to listen and respond to others help pupils develop confidence, fluency and accurate pronunciation.
Language immersion further strengthens learning. French is used extensively throughout the school day, and pupils experience Content and Language Integrated Learning (CLIL) through subjects such as PE and Art/DT, which are frequently taught in French. The French and francophone cultural experiences established in EYFS and Key Stage 1 continue throughout Key Stage 2 through daily songs, acts of worship and special calendar events.
Vocabulary enrichment is an important part of our curriculum. Pupils regularly learn, revisit and apply new vocabulary in a range of spoken and written contexts, enabling them to communicate with increasing accuracy and independence.
As an accredited DELF examination centre, we prepare pupils for internationally recognised DELF qualifications. Several members of staff are trained DELF examiners, ensuring that pupils benefit from expert preparation and guidance. Depending on their level of proficiency, pupils may work towards DELF Prim A1.1, DELF Prim A1 or DELF A2. By the end of Key Stage 2, pupils are expected to communicate in French with increasing confidence, accuracy and independence, ready for the next stage of their language-learning journey.
How is children’s learning in French assessed at St Jérôme?
Assessment is an integral part of French teaching and learning at St Jérôme. It enables teachers to identify pupils' strengths, address misconceptions and adapt teaching to meet individual needs.
Pupils are assessed regularly through a combination of formative and summative assessment. Ongoing assessment takes place during lessons through questioning, observation, speaking activities and written work. Weekly vocabulary tests help pupils to secure and retain new language.
In addition, pupils complete termly assessments linked to the Rachel Hawkes Scheme of Work, which assess progress in phonics, vocabulary and grammar. DELF-style assessments and practice papers are also used to prepare pupils for external examinations and to monitor progress across the four language skills: listening (compréhension orale), speaking (production orale), reading (compréhension des écrits) and writing (production écrite).
Assessment information is used to inform future teaching, support pupil progress and ensure that pupils are working within the most appropriate learning group. For many pupils, progress culminates in the successful completion of internationally recognised DELF qualifications.
Rachel Hawkes Scheme of Work
By Key Stage 2, most of our pupils have been introduced to the Rachel Hawkes Scheme of Work, upon which we build our French curriculum. Our wealth of francophone staff allows us to stream our French learning: just as Years 2 and 3 are split into three separate French ‘streamed’ levels, Years 4, 5 and 6 are split into four streamed levels. An individual pupils’ level is based on their current learning needs in French, rather than their year group or how long they have been learning French. The Schemes of Work draw on key recommendations from the pedagogy review and the Ofsted languages research report, which highlight the three key knowledge strands phonics, vocabulary, and grammar. They also exploit everyday and rich cultural contexts to build confident communication in the new language. The cyclical schemes are written with the four year groups of Key Stage 2 in mind: Year 3 - Rouge; Year 4 - Jaune; Year 5 - Bleu; and Year 6 - Vert. However, this is based on non-bilingual primary schools, so we begin the scheme in Year 2. The Schemes of Work, which have been written with the non-specialist teacher in mind, allow us to utilise the lessons and resources to suit our needs - we adapt, and ‘pick and choose’.
DELF Prim preparation
Most importantly, in terms of progression, the scheme gives us a very good basis. We add to these lessons, by using our bespoke activities built up from our range of resources, and lessons that will help pupils to prepare for the DELF Prim examinations, which can be taken in Year 4, 5 and/or 6. For example, Groupe Jaune (made up of mostly Year 4 pupils but also Y 5 and 6 pupils who need consolidation) will follow the Jaune (and progressing to Bleu) programme whilst also preparing for the DELF Prim A1.1 examination. Groupe Bleu will be working towards the DELF Prim A1 while utilising the Bleu / Vert scheme of work. Groupe Vert, mostly Year 6, some Year 5 and native French speakers will be working towards the DELF A2, using some resources beyond this in adapted foundation GCSE-level lessons.

Music
Subjects
Music
Music is a quintessential element of our bilingual education ethos as singing in French is part of our daily routines and seasonal celebrations from Reception onwards. We are currently developing musicianship at St. Jérôme by including some of the ideas of Zoltán Kodály, a Hungarian composer and educator who said:
“Let us take our children seriously! Everything follows from this…. only the best is good enough for a child!”
Kodály believed in developing the inner ear through singing exercises that follow hand signals for each note of the scale and repeating rhythmic patterns with sounds. This links very well with our approach to language acquisition and as stated in the National Curriculum, we agree that ”Music is a universal language.”
At St. Jérôme we are proud to have been recognised by Music Mark, following our nomination from Harrow Music Service in 2021 in recognition of a commitment to providing a high-quality music education for all children.
Music Mark is the UK Association for Music Education; they champion and support access to music for all children and young people.
“Music Mark works to enable our members, and the wider music education sector, to deliver high-quality musical and social outcomes for all children and young people. We would like to thank you for all the hard work your school does to support our collective vision.”
How We Teach Music At Saint Jérôme
In EYFS and KS1 we use the Stave House method. This method teaches children to read, play and write music. It uses a series of creative characters to engage children, through storytelling and songs. Children embark on a wonderful imaginary journey into the world of Stave House where they will be equipped with classical music skills for life, teaching them to read, write and play music. Stave House lays a musical foundation that is taught via a ‘see, hear, do ‘interactive approach to learning.
At St. Jérôme the KS2 classes follow the award winning Charanga Model Music to enable us to deliver the National Curriculum for Music. All children are given the opportunity to learn to play the recorder.
Please see the Music Curriculum Map which shows what we are working on each term and how we use our skills learnt in the classroom to perform at school events.

Art
Subjects
Curriculum Vision Statement:
At St Jérôme, children experience Art through a creative and inspiring curriculum that encourages curiosity, imagination, and self-expression. Through exploring a range of materials, techniques, and processes, pupils develop confidence in communicating their ideas and responding thoughtfully to the world around them.
Children develop key artistic skills in drawing, painting, sculpture, printing, and mixed media. They learn to experiment with colour, line, shape, texture, form, and pattern while refining their techniques and developing control in the use of different materials and tools. Pupils study the work of a diverse range of artists, craftspeople, and designers, enabling them to understand how art reflects different cultures, experiences, and periods of history. They are encouraged to observe closely, think critically, evaluate their work, and use sketchbooks to develop and refine their ideas.
As they progress through the school, children build their knowledge of artistic processes and vocabulary, becoming increasingly confident in creating original artwork and discussing their creative choices.
The end point for pupils is to leave St Jérôme as confident, creative, and reflective artists who can communicate ideas visually, apply a range of artistic techniques with skill, and evaluate their own work thoughtfully. They will have developed an appreciation of art and design and understand the contribution artists make to society and culture.
How is Art & Design taught at St Jérome?
At St Jérôme, Art & Design is taught through a creative, practical, and knowledge-rich curriculum that inspires curiosity, imagination, and self-expression. Lessons are taught primarily through the medium of French using a CLIL (Content and Language Integrated Learning) approach, enabling children to develop artistic skills whilst building confidence in understanding and using French in a meaningful context.
Teaching combines direct instruction, teacher modelling, practical exploration, discussion, and evaluation. Children study the work of artists, craftspeople, architects, and designers from a range of cultures and historical periods, developing an understanding of the role and impact of art in society. Pupils use sketchbooks as an important part of the creative process, recording observations, experimenting with techniques, developing ideas, and reflecting on their work over time. Sketchbooks provide opportunities for children to take risks, revisit learning, and see their artistic development across the curriculum.
Throughout the curriculum, pupils develop skills in drawing, painting, sculpture, printing, and mixed media. They learn to use the visual elements of art, including colour, line, shape, form, texture, pattern, and space, while generating, refining, and evaluating their own creative ideas. Children build knowledge of artistic techniques and processes and learn to analyse and discuss artwork using appropriate vocabulary.
Oracy is embedded throughout Art & Design. Through the CLIL approach, children regularly discuss artwork, explain their creative choices, and evaluate their own and others’ work using both artistic and French vocabulary. Structured talk and collaborative activities help pupils develop confidence in speaking, listening, and articulating their ideas.
By the end of Key Stage 2, pupils are able to create original artwork, apply a range of artistic techniques with skill and control, evaluate creative outcomes thoughtfully, and demonstrate an appreciation of significant artists, architects, and designers.
How is children’s learning in Art & Design assessed at St Jérôme?
At St Jérôme, assessment in Art & Design is ongoing, formative, and focused on the development of knowledge, skills, and creativity over time. Teachers assess children’s progress through observation, discussion, questioning, and the review of sketchbook work and final outcomes.
Sketchbooks play a central role in assessment, providing evidence of pupils’ developing ideas, experimentation with techniques, refinement of skills, and reflective thinking. They allow teachers to track progression in both artistic understanding and technical ability, as well as the development of creativity and independence.
Children’s learning is assessed against age-appropriate expectations, with a focus on key knowledge and skills such as drawing, painting, sculpture, and use of artistic techniques including line, shape, form, colour, texture, and pattern. Teachers also assess pupils’ ability to evaluate and discuss artwork using appropriate vocabulary, including during oracy-based activities linked to the CLIL approach in French.
Assessment is used to inform teaching and ensure that all pupils are supported and challenged appropriately. Feedback is given verbally during lessons and through dialogue while looking in sketchbooks, encouraging pupils to reflect, refine, and improve their work.
By the end of Key Stage 2, assessment ensures that pupils have developed a secure understanding of artistic techniques, can confidently express and evaluate their ideas, and have built a portfolio of work that demonstrates their progress, creativity, and achievement in Art & Design.

Computing
Subjects
Computing
Curriculum vision statement
At St Jérôme, children experience computing as a practical, creative and purposeful subject. Computing lessons give children opportunities to solve problems, build digital confidence, work collaboratively and talk clearly about their ideas, choices and solutions.
Our curriculum is built around three connected strands: computer science, information technology and digital literacy.
Online safety is taught throughout the curriculum. Children learn how to protect their identity, question online information, communicate appropriately and seek help when something feels wrong.
By the end of their time at St Jérôme, children are working towards becoming confident, responsible and creative users of technology. They should be able to explain how digital systems work, create digital content for different purposes, solve problems using computational thinking, and make safe choices online. Our aim is that children leave primary school ready to participate actively in a digital world.
How is computing taught at St Jerome?
Computing is taught through a sequenced curriculum, adapted from Teach Computing, and through meaningful use of technology across school life. Children learn through modelling, guided practice, discussion and practical tasks. Lessons include opportunities to plan, test, debug, improve and explain their work. Oracy is embedded by asking children to use subject vocabulary, discuss strategies, justify choices, present outcomes and evaluate digital work with others.
How is children’s learning in computing assessed at St Jerome?
Children’s learning in computing is assessed through questioning, observation, discussion and review of their digital projects. A specialist teacher looks at how well children use key vocabulary, apply taught skills, solve problems, debug, explain their choices and use technology safely and responsibly. In creative projects, children help build clear success criteria as part of the learning journey. These criteria are then used to guide, review and improve their work. Assessment focuses not only on the final product, but also on children’s thinking, independence, collaboration and ability to evaluate and refine their ideas.

Geography
Subjects
Geography
Now, more than ever, the current generation will be able to make significant changes to the environment we live in. At St Jerome, we wholeheartedly believe in giving children the opportunity through practical and theoretical experiences to discover the importance of the natural-world. As we strive to improve the way we live and to become more sustainable, knowledge will be key in securing a greener, more sustainable future for generations to come.
At St Jerome, geographical knowledge and skills are progressive and sequenced to provide a unique geographical journey throughout the Key Stages that unveils a robust curriculum, based on the National Curriculum, accessible to every pupil whilst high expectations are maintained. We take the opportunity to create links between all subjects to help solidify the learning taking place. We alternate our Geography and History topics ensuring that our children receive a well rounded teaching of the humanities subjects throughout the year as these subjects are interrelated. Children journal, as a chance to showcase their learning in a way that is memorable to them. Maps are displayed throughout the school and teachers and children are encouraged to use these when appropriate during all lessons to help to develop an awareness of the natural environment and physical landscapes, the study of people, places and cultures.
At St Jerome, we celebrate the importance of geography and its impact on our lives, help children to develop a sense of responsibility for the world and their place in it, aspire to discover more and be the change we want to see in the world for our future generations.
The curriculum builds a knowledge of:
Overview
Geography in EYFS
In EYFS, as an important part of the ‘Understanding the World’ strand of the curriculum, pupils explore the world through the topics Let’s Explore, Ready Steady Grow and On the Beach.
Geography in Key Stage 1
In Key Stage 1, each autumn term begins with essential skills and knowledge projects (Our Wonderful World in Year 1 and Let’s Explore the World in Year 2). In these topics, children learn critical geographical concepts, aspects, skills and knowledge. Throughout Key Stage 1, progression in learning is developed through topics such as Our Wonderful World; Let’s Explore the World; Bright Lights, Big City and Coastline. These topics allow for exploration of contrasting environments.
Geography in Key Stage 2
Throughout Key Stage 2, pupils begin each year with a topic to build their essential skills and knowledge. These include: One Planet, Our World; Interconnected World; Investigating Our World and Our Changing World. Key Stage 2 also allows pupils to explore physical features of geography in more detail in the topics Rocks, Relics and Rumbles; Misty Mountain, Winding River; Sow, Grow and Farm and Frozen Kingdoms.

History
Subjects
History
Curriculum Vision Statement:
Our History curriculum inspires children to develop a deep understanding of themselves, their communities and the wider world by exploring how the past shapes the present. Beginning in EYFS through meaningful exploration of people, places and change, pupils progressively build historical knowledge and understanding throughout their school journey.
Through the study of significant individuals, monarchs, civilisations and historical periods, children develop the core disciplinary skills of comparison, significance and causation. They learn to analyse change over time, evaluate similarities and differences, and understand the impact that people, events and ideas have had on society. By exploring humankind, creativity, and the influence of place and space, pupils gain insight into how cultures, communities and nations have evolved and interacted.
Our curriculum fosters curiosity, critical thinking, communication and historical enquiry, encouraging children to ask questions, challenge assumptions and form evidence-based conclusions. Through engaging end points, including presentations, assemblies and responses to thought-provoking Big Questions, pupils learn to articulate their understanding with confidence and connect historical learning to contemporary Britain and the wider world.
We aim to nurture informed, reflective and responsible citizens who appreciate the richness of our shared heritage and recognise history as a powerful tool for understanding the world today and shaping the future.
How is history taught at St Jerome?
In EYFS, as an important part of the ‘Understanding the World’ strand of the curriculum, pupils explore the world through the topics: Me and My Community, Once Upon a Time, Starry Night, Dangerous Dinosaurs, Long Ago and Big Wide World.
History in Key Stage 1
In Key Stage 1, children will explore a specific topic each Autumn and Summer. In Year 1 children will begin to understand themselves by exploring the topic Childhood, in which they will create timelines of their own lives alongside a family tree to form an understanding of significant events and the idea of causation. This topic includes a look at childhood in the 1950’s to allow the pupils to begin to compare and contrast as a key historical skill. This skill will then be improved upon in the Summer Term with the topic School Days where the children will think about their school days now alongside what life was like for a Victorian school child.
In Year 2, the children will focus on the idea of significance and what makes somebody significant on a large scale. In the Autumn term, they will first look at significant people in the topic Movers and Shakers in which the children will explore the impact of explorers and activists. In the Summer term, they will then begin to look at the significance and power of rulers with a specific focus on the British monarchy in the topic Magnificent Monarchs.
History in Key Stage 2
Throughout Key Stage 2, students will build on these skills of comparison, significance and causation through investigating specific eras or civilisations. There will be two focuses per year again one in Autumn term and the other in the Summer term. Similarly, the focus of History as a way of understanding the present will be explored in each topic to foster the idea that History allows oneself to understand their present.
End Points
During Key Stage 1, the pupils will work towards mini-end points that focus on a specific skill: for example, creating a timeline of monarchs (Comparison) or choosing their most significant figure (Movers and Shakers) and explaining their choice (Significance).
During Key Stage 2, there will be two end points to work towards. In one topic, the end point is an assembly where, in groups, the pupils present their learning (Oracy) to the rest of the school/ KS2 and parents. In the other topic, the children will answer a Big Question that aims to capture all of the learning of the topic and link it to modern day Britain/ world.

Mathematics
Subjects
Mathematics
At St Jérôme School our teaching of Mathematics is based on the programme of study set in the National Curriculum for England.
The National Curriculum’s three overarching aims - that all children become fluent in the fundamentals of mathematics and are thus equipped to reason mathematically and solve problems - are central to our approach to the teaching of mathematics.
We prioritise the development of children’s number sense as the foundation that will enable children to become fluent in the fundamentals of mathematics. This involves ensuring our children develop both factual and procedural fluency and conceptual understanding in tandem.
Procedural fluency refers to the rapid, accurate, flexible and efficient recall and application of facts and procedures. We aim to ensure our children will become increasingly fluent through practice within every lesson; in addition, this academic year we will be implementing weekly low stakes practice tests that will allow children to consolidate their recall of number bonds and times tables, following a progression from EYFS through to year 6.
Conceptual understanding refers to children having a knowledge of underpinning mathematical structure and relationships. Our teachers give careful thought to the concrete and pictorial representations, as well as the precise mathematical language that will allow our children to deepen their knowledge and understanding of abstract concepts (see below).
We aim to develop our children’s ability to move fluently between different representations of mathematical ideas and thus will increasingly see mathematics as an interconnected subject.
For example, children will develop a depth of understanding of the number 12 through moving between the following, along with other, representations:
Representations are displayed on working walls for children to continually refer back to throughout each unit of work.
Key vocabulary is routinely shared with children and displayed on working walls within the lesson. Stem sentences are utilised to support children’s own use of language and to reinforce their understanding of mathematical structure and relationships. For example:
If the whole is divided into ( ) equal parts, then each part is ( ) of the whole.
Opportunities for children to reason and problem solve are present in every lesson. Throughout lessons, teachers facilitate mathematical discussions with pupils, encouraging them to follow lines of enquiry, conjecture relationships and generalisations, and develop arguments, justification or proof using mathematical language as appropriate for the year group. When working in their books, children are encouraged to record their thinking process, as well as their solutions, through jottings, diagrams and words.
Depth and Challenge
Our teaching provides all children with the opportunity to develop a deep understanding of mathematical concepts. Those who grasp concepts rapidly are challenged through being offered rich and sophisticated problems before any acceleration through new content. This takes the form of the ‘now think really hard’ task provided within every lesson. Children may be selected for supplementary enrichment opportunities including the First Mathematics Challenge, Primary Mathematics Challenge, and the Count on Us Primary Maths Challenge.
Assessment
First and foremost, ongoing formative assessment takes place throughout the course of each lesson as teachers check for understanding, address misconceptions and provide feedback to pupils in the moment. Students’ books are marked in accordance with our marking and feedback policy. Children’s attainment and progress over longer periods of time will be assessed through end of unit progress checks.
Long-term Plans
We follow the White Rose Maths schemes of learning. In addition to the White Rose materials we draw on a range of high quality resources to support our lesson planning, including the NCETM Primary Mastery Professional Development materials and hard copies of Singaporean textbooks.
For further details on what is taught please click the link for the relevant year group. Details of the Mathematics taught in Reception can be found on the EYFS page.
Please note that these long-term plans are a guide and that teachers, from time to time, will use their professional judgement to move more quickly through the curriculum or to spend more time consolidating a concept.

Reading
Subjects
Reading
The Development of Reading at St. Jérôme CoE Bilingual School
Our aim is for all of our pupils to develop reading fluency alongside strong comprehension and preferences for wide-ranging, challenging reading material – children who can effectively read to learn as well as read willingly for its inherent pleasure. We believe that children need to read with fluency and understanding to be successful throughout their education and beyond into adulthood. We know that children whose parents/carers regularly read with their children and enjoy conversations about books they have chosen are hugely advantaged and, unless a child has a specific reading difficulty, will make faster progress then those children who do not have those opportunities. We vision our school to be a place where we take positive action to fill this gap in opportunity and enable all children to leave our school equipped with the reading skills to give them the best educational chances. The strategy with which we believe will best deliver this vision has been researched in depth. We acknowledge the 2009 Rose Review’s support of the Simple View of Reading (appendix 1) and the need to build strong synthetic phonics foundations for reading development, which is why we have recently embraced the Phonics Bug Synthetic phonics program. Around and alongside this, we aim to develop children’s vocabulary and comprehension skills. We know that comprehension supports the decoding process and is also the end goal of reading that enables children to become book lovers, who engage in wide-ranging and challenging texts. Religious Education
Subjects
Religious Education
In Church of England schools, where pupils and staff come from all faiths and none, religious education (RE) is a highly valued academic subject that enables understanding of how religion and beliefs affect our lives. At the heart of RE in church schools is the teaching of Christianity and pupils also learn about other faiths and world views.
Our approach to Religious Education is based on the following Church of England guidance. You can view this guidance here:
Statement of Entitlement 219 KB Key Principles of a Balanced Curriculum in RE 255 KB
At St Jérôme Church of England School we teach children about Christianity and also the other faiths that are represented in our local community.

Science
Subjects
Science
Curriculum Vision Statement
At St Jerome, we believe that science underpins a thirst for knowledge and understanding of how and why the natural and physical world works. Science has changed our lives and is vital to the world’s prosperity and our ambitious curriculum is planned as a 7-year journey across the Primary School reflecting the need of developing inquisitive young scientists. The broad and balanced nature of the subject ensures that all children are able to access the learning and children are encouraged to recognise the power of rational explanation and develop a sense of excitement and curiosity about natural phenomena. Our children leave school in Year 6 with the skills necessary to continue developing further.
Investigations are planned with the children’s curiosity in mind whilst also meeting the ‘Working Scientifically’ aspects of the National Curriculum. National Winners of the French Pop Video Competition
We are delighted to announce that Saint Jérôme has been crowned National Winner in the 7–11 age category of the French Pop Video Competition, organised by Francophonie UK in partnership with the Institut Français du Royaume-Uni and supported by TV5 Monde. Four pupils attended the awards ceremony at the Institut Français in London, where they proudly accepted a trophy and a collection of French books for the school library.
The award recognises the creativity, teamwork and commitment behind our project, « 10 Bougies Pour Notre École », created to celebrate the school’s 10th birthday. Congratulations to all the pupils, staff and parents who helped write, perform and produce the winning entry. You can watch the video here: 10 Bougies Pour Notre École.

Design & Technology
Subjects
Design & Technology
Curriculum Vision Statement:
At St Jérôme, Design and Technology (D&T) is a practical, creative, and purposeful subject taught through the medium of French as part of our CLIL (Content and Language Integrated Learning) approach. Children experience D&T through engaging, hands-on projects that encourage them to explore real-world problems, think creatively, and bring their ideas to life through designing and making.
Teaching is carefully sequenced to develop key knowledge, skills, and concepts over time. Pupils are taught to design, make, and evaluate purposeful products for specific audiences and purposes. They develop skills in researching, generating ideas, planning, and communicating designs through discussion, sketches, and models. Children learn to select and use a range of tools, materials, and techniques safely and effectively, including mechanisms, structures, textiles, and food technology, depending on the project.
Throughout their learning, pupils develop an understanding of key design principles such as stability, strength, function, and purpose. They are encouraged to test, refine, and evaluate their ideas, learning from both success and failure.
By the end of Key Stage 2, pupils will be confident, independent designers who can apply their knowledge and skills to solve practical problems creatively. They will be able to generate and develop innovative ideas, use a range of tools and materials safely, evaluate their work thoughtfully, and communicate their design thinking effectively.
How is Design & Technology taught at St Jérome?
At St Jérôme, Design and Technology (D&T) is taught as a practical, creative, and purposeful subject through a CLIL (Content and Language Integrated Learning) approach, with lessons delivered with French input . This enables pupils to develop their design and making skills while also building confidence in using French in meaningful, real-life contexts.
Teaching is carefully sequenced and includes a range of pedagogical approaches such as modelling, direct instruction, investigation, collaborative work, hands-on experimentation, and iterative design. Pupils are encouraged to think like designers by exploring real-world problems, generating ideas, and testing and refining their solutions. They are taught to design, make, and evaluate purposeful products for specific audiences and needs.
Children develop key knowledge and skills across a range of areas, including structures, mechanisms, textiles, and food technology. They learn to use tools and materials safely and accurately, while developing an understanding of key design concepts such as function, stability, strength, and purpose. Pupils are also taught to plan, sketch, construct prototypes, and evaluate their work, making improvements based on testing and feedback.
Oracy is embedded throughout D&T through the CLIL approach. Pupils are encouraged to discuss ideas, explain design choices, justify decisions, and evaluate products using both technical vocabulary and French language. Structured talk, paired discussion, and group reflection help children to develop confidence in articulating their thinking clearly and collaboratively.
By the end of Key Stage 2, pupils will be confident, independent designers who can apply their knowledge and skills creatively to solve practical problems. They will be able to generate innovative ideas, use tools and materials safely and effectively, evaluate their work critically, and communicate their design thinking clearly.
How is children’s learning in Design & Technology assessed at St Jérôme?
At St Jérôme, assessment in Design and Technology (D&T) is ongoing, formative, and focused on the development of pupils’ knowledge, skills, and understanding over time. Teachers assess learning through observation, discussion, questioning, and the evaluation of pupils’ design and practical outcomes.
A key part of assessment is the design process itself, including pupils’ ability to generate ideas, plan, make, test, and evaluate their products. Evidence of learning is captured through sketchbooks, design plans, photographs, prototypes, and finished products, which show progression in both thinking and practical skills.
Children are assessed with a focus on key areas such as designing for a purpose, using tools and materials safely and accurately, and understanding key concepts such as structure, mechanism, stability, and function. Teachers verbally assess pupils’ ability to evaluate their work and suggest improvements based on testing and feedback.
Oral feedback is an important part of assessment, supported by the CLIL approach in French. Pupils are encouraged to explain their ideas, describe processes, and evaluate outcomes using appropriate vocabulary.
Assessment is used to inform future teaching and ensure that all pupils are supported and challenged appropriately. By the end of Key Stage 2, pupils will have developed a secure understanding of the design process, confidence in using tools and materials, and the ability to evaluate and improve their work thoughtfully and independently,
